svg.text: Everyday English - Grammar
Reduced relatives:
preserving modality
MEANING
A participle modifier can shorten a relative clause, but it
may lose modal meaning such as ability or permission.
IN CONTEXT
Analysts reviewing the figures are busy. Analysts who
can approve the budget are authorized; analysts
approving it are actually doing so.
USAGE NOTE
Do not replace "who can approve" with "approving":
ability or permission becomes an actual activity.
Likewise, "who must review" expresses an obligation
that "reviewing" does not preserve. Reduce a relative
only when the intended voice, time and modal meaning
remain clear.
CONVERSATION
A: Can I shorten "colleagues who can approve the
figures"?
B: "Colleagues approving the figures" changes the
meaning.
A: It describes what they are doing, rather than their
authority.
B: Exactly; keep the full relative clause to preserve
permission.
YOUR TURN
Does "staff reviewing the budget" preserve "staff who
must review the budget"? Model: No. The full clause
states an obligation; the participle describes an activity.
